title: What delivery guarantees does your message queue actually give you?
description: At-least-once vs at-most-once vs exactly-once, why duplicates are inevitable, and how consumers deduplicate.

data.text: Queues promise at-least-once, at-most-once, or exactly-once — and in practice you get at-least-once everywhere it matters. The subtle part: duplicates are not a queue malfunction, they are the cost of surviving crashes. If a consumer processes a message and crashes before acknowledging it, the broker cannot know the work happened — so it redelivers. Designing consumers as idempotent handlers converts 'at-least-once delivery' into 'exactly-once effect', which is the guarantee that actually reaches your business logic.

The interviewer is testing distributed-systems literacy: do you know why 'exactly-once' across a network is a marketing claim unless processing and acknowledgement are atomic, and can you describe the concrete idempotency machinery — dedup stores, idempotency keys, natural idempotency — that makes duplicates harmless.

items: At-most-once: fire and forget — the broker delivers what it can and drops on failure. No duplicates, but messages are lost on crash. Fine for metrics/telemetry, wrong for money.

At-least-once: acknowledge after processing; redeliver on failure/timeout. Nothing is lost, but everything can arrive twice (or more). This is Kafka's default for consumers, Azure Service Bus peek-lock, SQS standard, RabbitMQ manual ack.

Exactly-once: duplicates are prevented by making processing + acknowledgement atomic — transactional offset commits (Kafka within the consumer transaction boundary), deduplication windows (Service Bus in a transaction with the receive), or effectively-once via idempotent consumers. True exactly-once end-to-end (across your DB write AND the ack) still requires the consumer to participate.

data.title: Dedup key + processed-message table, in one transaction

items: Dedup store (above): universal, works with any broker, costs one table/Redis key per message.
Natural idempotency: 'set status = Shipped' is idempotent by shape; 'increment stock by 1' is not — prefer absolute state over deltas.
Idempotency keys from the producer: the caller supplies the key (payments APIs do this) — same key returns the original result instead of re-charging.
Transactional outbox on the producer side pairs with this: commit message + state atomically, relay publishes, broker delivers ≥ once, consumer dedups. That is the full loop.

Broker-native windows: Service Bus DeliveryCount/max-auto-relock and Kafka offset commits reduce duplicates but never eliminate the crash-between-effect-and-ack gap — the consumer-side dedup closes it.

data.title: Ack after the effect, never before
data.text: Acknowledging a message before committing its database write guarantees loss (crash after ack, before commit). Acknowledging after guarantees duplicates (crash after commit, before ack). You must choose loss or duplicates — duplicates are recoverable, loss is not — and then make duplicates harmless with idempotency.

items: Poison messages: cap DeliveryCount and move to a dead-letter queue — otherwise one bad message loops forever.
Visibility/lock timeout: a handler that runs longer than the lock loses it and gets redelivered mid-work — extend locks or shorten handlers.
Backlog alarms: queue depth and oldest-message age are your lag SLIs; alarm before users notice.
Partitioning: one aggregate per partition key preserves per-entity ordering while allowing parallelism across entities.
Retries interact with queues: consumer retries need backoff/jitter too — a tight redelivery loop is a retry storm with extra steps.

data.title: Key Takeaways
points: At-least-once is the realistic guarantee; duplicates are designed for, not bugs.
Never ack before the effect commits — choose recoverable duplicates over silent loss.
Idempotent consumers: unique dedup key + business write in one transaction.
Ordering needs partition keys and sequence checks; dedup alone doesn't reorder.
data.takeaway: Queues deliver at least once — your consumer makes it exactly once by making every message's effect idempotent and atomic with its dedup record.
